lesson.title: Him & Whom Proof Texts
lesson.subtitle: Spot the ancient nasal in English — then mirror it in mich, dich, ihn, wen

hook.title: The Evidence Was In Your Mouth All Along
hook.content: You have been declining the accusative your whole life — in English. He saw me: me, not I. I saw him: him, not he. To whom: whom, not who. That final m is the ancient Indo-European object marker, and English pronouns still wear it. German wears the same marker, softened from m to n: mich (me), dich (thee), ihn (him), wen (whom). Every time you say 'whom', you are speaking German grammar with an m. Today: the proof texts.

footnotes.title: The m → n Softening
footnotes.content: Proto-Indo-European marked masculine accusatives with *-m. English kept the m (him, whom); High German softened unstressed final -m into -n (ihn, wen). Same marker, two pronunciations — one ancient law.

pattern.title: The Pronoun Proof Grid
pattern.content: Read the grid as evidence, not vocabulary: I ↔ ich, me ↔ mich; thou ↔ du, thee ↔ dich; he ↔ er, him ↔ ihn; who ↔ wer, whom ↔ wen. The English forms are not translations — they are the same words with the same job. And the feminine/neuter pair stays flat on both sides of the North Sea: she/her collapsed early, and German sie/sie, das/das never bothered. Witness statements: 'I see him' = Ich sehe ihn. 'Whom do you seek?' = Wen suchst du? — verb first, like Knowest thou?
pattern.linguist_note: wen ↔ whom is the cleanest pair: both carry the full nasal marker, one as -m, one as -n. wen suchst du? is the register of courtroom English 'whom do you seek?' — German never dropped whom.

exercises.prompt: Match each English objective pronoun with its German twin:
exercises.explanation: The same ancient nasal marker: English -m, German -n. One marker, two spellings.

exercises.prompt: Why does German 'wen' end in -n while English 'whom' ends in -m?
options: High German softened the ancient final -m into -n
wen and whom are unrelated words
German pronouns have no case marker
exercises.target_answer: High German softened the ancient final -m into -n
exercises.explanation: Same Indo-European marker *-m: English kept it crisp (him, whom), German blurred it to -n (ihn, wen).

exercises.prompt: What English pronoun is the direct twin of 'ihn'?
exercises.explanation: er → ihn is he → him: the same pronoun, with the nasal softened to n on the German side.

exercises.prompt: Complete the Case × Person matrix for the accusative ('me'):
exercises.row_law: Row: Case role (Nominative subject vs. Accusative direct object)
exercises.column_law: Column: Person (ich-family I/me vs. du-family thou/thee)
exercises.meaning: me (accusative of ich — English 'me' wears the same nasal)
exercises.explanation: ich → mich and du → dich: the object case adds the nasal English still wears in 'me' and 'thee'. [Ref: ihn]

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I see him and he sees me'
exercises.target_answer: Ich sehe ihn und er sieht mich
exercises.meaning: I see him and he sees me

vocab_hints.note: sehen → er sieht — the vowel wanders, as in see/saw

exercises.explanation: Two clauses mirror each other: ich sehe ihn / er sieht mich — both direct objects wearing the nasal.

summary.outcome: Use mich, dich, ihn, wen as objects — and hear English whom as German grammar with an m.

use_example.german: Ich sehe ihn und er sieht mich.
use_example.english: I see him and he sees me.

summary.takeaway: The accusative nasal survives in English him/me/thee/whom and German ihn/mich/dich/wen — one marker, two spellings.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the articles are pronouns in disguise — die is D- plus sie, der is D- plus er, das is D- plus es.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Him & Whom Proof Texts (I see him and he sees me):
twist.target_answer: Ich sehe ihn und er sieht mich
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich sehe ihn und er sieht mich" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Him & Whom Proof Texts without relying on short-term echo.

du.etymology_derivation: Direct cognate of archaic English "thou". Conjugates with -st (thou goest ↔ du gehst).

die.etymology_derivation: th → d. Sounds identical to emphatic English "thee".

das.shift_rule: TH → D + T → S / SS / Z
das.etymology_derivation: Double shift: th → d and final t → s.

finden.context_translation: I cannot find it / I find it not.
finden.etymology_derivation: Stem find + infinitive -en (German keeps pure short [ɪ] vowel).

frost.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *frost — the same word as English frost. [wiktionary]

klima.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin clima — a shared Latin loan both languages made separately. [wiktionary]

stiefel.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Old French estivel; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

hilfe.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *helpō, from helpaną (to help, already known) — the ancestor of English help. [wiktionary]

wichtig.context_phrase: Wasser ist wichtig für die Gesundheit.
wichtig.etymology_derivation: From the root of Gewicht (weight) plus -ig; the entry itself compares English weighty, which builds importance out of weight with the very same metaphor. [wiktionary]

dose.context_translation: The can is in the kitchen cabinet.
dose.etymology_derivation: Probably from Latin dosis via Middle Low German dose; the sense moved from a dose of medicine to the container that holds it, and English dose is the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

nur.etymology_derivation: Contracted from Old High German niwāri, literally were it not (ni 'not' + wāri 'were'); Old English had the same word nǣre — from if-not to only. [wiktionary]

paket.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French paquet — the same French bundle-word behind English packet. [wiktionary]

handwerk.context_translation: My uncle is learning a trade.
handwerk.etymology_derivation: Hand + Werk — Proto-Germanic *handuwerką; the entry points to English handiwork, and Werk carries the PIE *werǵ- root of work. [wiktionary]
